lesson.title: Wohnen I: das Zimmer, die Wohnung, der Flur, der Keller, die Etage
lesson.subtitle: the rooms of a flat — and the twin hiding inside English timber

hook.title: The Room and the Timber
hook.content: das Zimmer and English timber are the same Proto-Germanic word, *timrą — the building material. English kept the boards; German shifted the T to a Z-sound (the zehn/two shift) and kept the meaning 'room', because a room is what the timber builds. die Wohnung is wohnen's noun, the place where the living happens. der Keller is a Roman import both languages share: Latin cellarium became German Keller and English cellar. die Etage came from French étage — and English stage is its doublet, both from Old French estage, a 'standing place', which is why a stage is where actors stand and an Etage is where a flat stands. der Flur looks like floor, and the two may be distant cousins — but the trail is muddy, so treat the resemblance as a hint, not a proof. English lost the twin, if it ever had one.

footnotes.title: One Head Noun, Four Rooms
footnotes.content: German builds rooms with a compound engine: das Wohnzimmer (living room, wohnen + Zimmer), das Schlafzimmer (schlafen + Zimmer), das Badezimmer (Bad + Zimmer), das Esszimmer (essen + Zimmer). Learn das Zimmer once and four rooms come free.

pattern.title: Where the Rooms Stand
pattern.content: Position words do the navigating. 1. With sein: Der Keller ist dort unten (the basement is down there), Das Zimmer ist oben (the room is up top). 2. gegenüber after the noun: Das Haus gegenüber ist alt (the house opposite is old) — no preposition, the word leans back on its noun. 3. die Nähe with in: Der Markt ist in der Nähe (the market is nearby), Das Sofa ist in der Nähe vom Fenster (the sofa is near the window) — and the opposite is weit: der Weg ist weit (the way is far). 4. The compound engine: das Wohnzimmer, das Schlafzimmer, das Badezimmer, das Esszimmer — one head noun, four different front halves.
pattern.linguist_note: *timrą meant 'material for building', and its verb *timrjan 'to build' survives in English 'to timber' — to brace something with beams. English kept the engineer's word; German narrowed the noun to the finished product: the room.

exercises.prompt: A flat, navigated — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The sofa is near the window
matching_pairs.german: Das Sofa ist in der Nähe vom Fenster

matching_pairs.english: My flat is big and bright
matching_pairs.german: Meine Wohnung ist groß und hell

matching_pairs.english: The shoes are standing in the hallway

exercises.target_answer: Der Keller ist dort unten, Das Haus gegenüber ist alt, Das Zimmer ist oben, Das Sofa ist in der Nähe vom Fenster, Meine Wohnung ist groß und hell, Die Schuhe stehen im Flur
exercises.meaning: a basement down there, a house opposite, a room up top, a sofa near the window, a big bright flat, shoes in the hallway
exercises.explanation: Five rooms and four position words. gegenüber follows its noun like an afterthought, and die Schuhe stehen im Flur is where German boots live — standing, not lying, because stehen is the verb furniture prefers.

exercises.prompt: Which of these rooms wears the T→Z badge that turned English timber into its German twin?
exercises.meaning: das Zimmer ↔ timber: the T→Z shift inside a doublet
exercises.explanation: *timrą kept its T in English timber and hardened it to a Z-sound in German Zimmer — the same law that made zwei out of two and zehn out of ten. One word became the material in English and the room in German. der Keller and die Etage are Latin and French imports, and der Flur's trail goes cold.

exercises.prompt: der Keller is German's borrowing of Latin cellarium — give the English word that borrowed the same Latin:
exercises.meaning: der Keller ↔ cellar — both from Latin cellarium
exercises.explanation: Latin cellarium, a store-room, was borrowed whole by German (der Keller) and by English (cellar). And die Etage has its own doublet: French étage and English stage both come from Old French estage — English just kept the S.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the distance sentence: 'The market is nearby, the way is far'
exercises.target_answer: Der Markt ist in der Nähe, der Weg ist weit
exercises.meaning: The market is nearby, the way is far
exercises.explanation: in der Nähe is the fixed frame for 'nearby' — die Nähe always wears in der here — and weit answers it from the other end. der Weg is the same word family as German's way-verbs: the road you walk every day.

das Schlafzimmer is schlafen + Zimmer, built by the compound engine — and das Badezimmer in the bank shows the same engine again. Stack the position words: dort oben, dort unten — German lets them pile up in that order.

summary.outcome: Name the rooms, place them with oben, unten, dort and gegenüber, and say what is in der Nähe and what is weit.

use_example.german: Der Keller ist dort unten — das Schlafzimmer ist oben.
use_example.english: The basement is down there — the bedroom is up top.

summary.takeaway: Zimmer is timber's shifted twin (T→Z), Keller and cellar share Latin cellarium, Etage and stage share estage — and das Schlafzimmer builds itself from schlafen + Zimmer.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the things inside the rooms — der Teppich, der Schrank, der Spiegel, der Vorhang, der Balkon — and a wardrobe related to English shrink.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Wohnen I: das Zimmer, die Wohnung, der Flur, der Keller, die Etage (The bedroom is up there):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Das Schlafzimmer ist dort oben" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Wohnen I: das Zimmer, die Wohnung, der Flur, der Keller, die Etage without relying on short-term echo.

zimmer.context_phrase: Mein Zimmer ist groß und hell.
zimmer.context_translation: My room is big and bright.
zimmer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *timrą — cognate with English timber: English keeps t, German shifted it to z. [wiktionary]

wohnung.context_phrase: Meine Wohnung ist im dritten Stock.
wohnung.context_translation: My apartment is on the third floor.
wohnung.etymology_derivation: Wohnen (to dwell) plus -ung; the page documents the archaic English cognate woning (dwelling-place) from the same dwelling-word. [wiktionary]

flur.context_translation: The shoes are standing in the hallway.
flur.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic floraz; English floor is a direct cognate that kept the old sense, while German Flur narrowed to mean hallway. [wiktionary]

keller.context_translation: The bicycles are standing in the basement.
keller.etymology_derivation: From Old High German kellari, from West Germanic kellari, an early loan of Late Latin cellarium; English cellar is the same Latin word through Old French. [wiktionary]

etage.context_phrase: Wir wohnen in der dritten Etage.
etage.context_translation: We live on the third floor.
etage.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French étage; English stage is a doublet from the same Old French word estage. [wiktionary]

gegenüber.context_phrase: Der Supermarkt ist gegenüber der Bank.
gegenüber.context_translation: The supermarket is opposite the bank.
gegenüber.etymology_derivation: gegen + über — literally over-against; über is the twin of English over (both from PIE *upér) and gegen the twin of against. [wiktionary]

oben.context_phrase: Das Buch ist oben auf dem Tisch.
oben.context_translation: The book is up on the table.
oben.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ubanē, kin to über (over); no direct English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

unten.etymology_derivation: Old High German undenân, kin to unter (under); no direct English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

nähe.context_phrase: In der Nähe gibt es einen Markt.
nähe.etymology_derivation: nah + -e; nah is the twin of archaic English nigh. [wiktionary]

weit.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wīdaz — the direct cognate of English wide. [wiktionary]

sofa.context_translation: The sofa is in the living room.
sofa.etymology_derivation: From French sofa, ultimately Arabic ṣuffa — the same loan route as English sofa. [wiktionary]

fenster.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *fenestr, an early borrowing of Latin fenestra — a Latin loan both languages share. [wiktionary]

zinn.context_translation: The goblet is made of tin.

zuerst.context_phrase: Zuerst frühstücken wir, dann gehen wir.
zuerst.context_translation: First we have breakfast, then we go.
zuerst.etymology_derivation: zu + erst — zu is the twin of to (t → z) and erst the Germanic earliest, kept in archaic English erstwhile. [wiktionary]

ausländer.etymology_derivation: Ausland + -er, from Middle High German uzlender; the page lists English outlander and outlandish as cognates — literally an out-lander. [wiktionary]

zweifel.context_phrase: Ich habe Zweifel an dem Plan.
zweifel.context_translation: I have doubts about the plan.
zweifel.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *twifl, related to the root of zwei, two — being of two minds; English doubt did the same, from Latin dubitare, literally to be of two (duo). [wiktionary][etymonline]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
